en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Son Śyāma, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Shengjian of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Virāḍha with twelve hundred and fifty [monks].
Ten bhikṣus, along with a multitude of bodhisattvas, kings, ministers, elders, householders, and incalculable numbers of faithful men and women, gathered together at one time.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you, remain in meditative concentration and listen!

In my previous lives, when I first attained the path of a bodhisattva, I was fully endowed with the practice of the precepts; with single-minded diligence, I cultivated and accumulated wisdom and skillful means. My accumulated merits were beyond measure, such that none among the devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, or common people were able to emulate them."
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his hands joined in *añjali*, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to hear what you would say.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a Bodhisattva named Sarvācāra-sundara. Compassionate and benevolent, he bestowed gifts and rescued all living beings; he constantly practiced the four immeasurable minds, delivered the world from perils and hardships, and nurtured those who suffered."

In the Tuṣita Heaven, he instructs the devas, constantly maintaining a concentrated mind during three periods of both day and night to contemplate samādhi, illuminating and observing the paths of good and evil among the people throughout the ten directions of the world.

Knowing those who recognize the existence of father and son, who are filial and obedient to their parents, who serve the Three Honored Ones, who are respectful and compliant toward their teachers and elders, and who cultivate various meritorious virtues, he constantly surveys the five realms of existence everywhere with his divine eye.

At that time, there was a country called Kāśī, where lived an elder who was solitary and without sons; both his eyes were blind. His heart’s wish was to enter the mountains to seek a decisive realization of the unsurpassed path, to cultivate pure resolve, and to take faith and delight in seclusion.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"This person has resolved to study the wondrous Way, yet both his eyes are blind; with no sight, he might enter the mountains and fall into a ravine or pit, or encounter venomous insects that would bring him harm."
"If my life comes to an end, I shall become their son and provide for my parents until the end of their years.
Thereupon, when the Bodhisattva’s lifespan was exhausted, he descended to be born into the home of blind parents and became their son.
The parents loved him with profound joy and affection. Originally, they had resolved to seek the Way and enter the mountains, but because he had been born to them, they took pleasure in the world.
When the son reached the age of ten, he was named Śyāma. He was supremely filial, benevolent, and compassionate, practicing the ten wholesome actions:

refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, deception, drinking intoxicants, false speech, frivolous talk, and envy; he followed the Way without doubt and was diligent day and night. He served his parents as one serves Heaven. His speech was always accompanied by a smile, never harming another's feelings; his conduct accorded with the Dharma, never leaning toward partiality. Thereupon, the parents were filled with great joy and no longer had any sorrow.
When Śyāma had reached the age of ten, he knelt upright and said to his parents:
"I have originally resolved upon the Great Intention to enter the deep mountains, seeking the empty, tranquil, and unsurpassed Way. How could I abandon my fundamental vow for the sake of a son?"

Human life in this world is subject to a hundred changes and lacks permanence; one's life is not of stone or metal, and its end approaches without fixed date. I wish for you to fulfill my original intention and follow my former resolve: let us go together with our parents into the mountains to attend to their needs, ensuring we do not miss the proper season.
The parents replied to Śyāma, saying, "Your filial piety Heaven itself knows; if you do not violate your original vow, you may then enter the mountains.
Śyāma immediately gave away all the possessions in his home to the poor and destitute of the kingdom, and then entered the mountains together with his parents.
"When Śyāma reached the mountains, he made a hut for his parents out of reeds, provided them with beds and mats, and ensured they were always at ease, being neither cold nor hot."

It has been exactly one year since he entered the mountains, and all the fruits have become abundant and exquisite; they are fragrant and sweet when eaten, and spring water gushes forth, pure and cool.
Within the ponds, lotuses of five colors bloom with brilliant clarity, and the blended fragrance of sandalwood trees is so lush that its scent is twice as strong as usual.

The winds and rains come in their proper seasons; it is neither cold nor hot. The leaves of the trees join together to shield against the rain and dew, and by covering the sunlight, the area beneath them remains perpetually cool.
Flying birds gathered and alighted, all producing the sounds of music to entertain his blind parents;

lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, wolves, and venomous insects all turned toward one another with hearts of compassion, harboring no intent to alarm or harm. They all drank water and ate fruit, their hearts free from any further fear. Deer and various birds all came to stay nearby, their voices harmonizing with those of Śyāma to entertain his blind parents.

Śyāma was supremely filial, benevolent, and compassionate beyond reproach; he walked upon the earth ever fearing it might suffer pain. The celestial deities and mountain spirits all assumed human forms to console and comfort the three practitioners day and night; with single-minded concentration and settled intent, they were free from further sorrow or anxiety.
"Śyāma constantly gathered a hundred kinds of fruits and melons with his parents to feed them.

When his parents were thirsty and wished to drink, Śyāma would put on his deer-skin garment, carry a pitcher, and go to fetch water; even the wild deer and flying birds would come to drink there, feeling no fear or hesitation."
At that time, the King of Kāśī entered the mountains to hunt. Seeing deer and birds by the water’s edge, the king drew his bow and shot at them; however, his arrow mistakenly struck Śyāma.
Śyāma, being struck by a poisoned arrow and suffering great pain, cried out loudly, saying:
"Who has taken a single poisoned arrow and shot and killed three practitioners of the Way?
Hearing the sound of a human voice, the king dismounted his horse and went before Śyāma; Śyāma then said to the king:

"Elephants die because of their tusks; rhinoceroses die because of their horns; peacocks die because of their plumage; and deer die because of their hides. Now, I am dead without tusks, without horns, without plumage, and without hide or flesh—unfit for consumption. What crime have I committed that I should be shot and killed so pointlessly?"
The king said, "Who are you?
You are dressed in deer skin and are no different from birds and beasts."
Śyāma said, "I am a man from this king's realm;

I have come with my blind parents to study the Way for more than twenty years, and never before have I been harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous insects. Now, however, I have been struck and killed by the King’s arrow."

"At that moment, a great violent wind arose within the mountain, blowing and breaking the trees; birds, beasts, lions, bears, *pī*, tigers, wolves, and venomous creatures all cried out, shaking the entire mountain.
The sun lost its brilliance, the flowing springs went dry, the various flowers withered and died, and thunder and lightning shook the earth."
At that time, the blind parents suddenly rose in alarm and said, "What strange occurrence is this?
Śāṇa has been gone for a long time fetching water and has not yet returned; could it be that he has been harmed by venomous insects?"

"The birds and beasts cry out in lamentation, their voices wailing unlike those of ordinary times; winds arise from all four directions and the trees snap and break. There must be some calamitous anomaly.
At that time, the king was struck with fear and deeply reproached himself:

"I originally went to hunt deer, but by mistake my arrow wounded and killed this practitioner of the Way. This sin is exceedingly heavy; because of my greed for a small amount of meat, I have incurred such a grave disaster."
"I shall now save my son's life by offering the wealth and treasures of the entire kingdom, his palaces, courtesans, hamlets, and cities.

At that time, the king stepped forward and pulled the arrow from Śyama’s chest with his hand; the arrow was so deeply embedded that it could not be extracted. Birds and beasts gathered from all directions like clouds, wailing and crying out in such a way that they shook the entire mountain.
The king became even more terrified, his limbs trembling all over. Śyāma said, "This is not the fault of the King! It is brought about by my own past karma.

I do not begrudge my own life, but I pity my blind parents; they are already advanced in years and have no sight. If I were to perish suddenly, they too would surely die of grief. It is for this reason that I am so distressed and tormented."
At that moment, all the devas, nāgas, and spirits were deeply moved.
The king spoke again with renewed resolve:
"I would rather enter the hells and suffer punishment for a hundred kalpas than allow Śyama’s life to be restored."
Kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he turned toward Śyāma and repented:

"If Śyāma’s life should come to an end, I shall no longer return to my kingdom, but will instead remain in these mountains to provide for your blind parents just as you did when you were alive. Do not harbor any resentment. May the devas, nāgas, and spirits all bear witness that I do not violate this vow."
When Śyāma heard the king’s vow, he said:

"Though I am struck by a poisoned arrow, my heart is joyful and my mind is glad; even in death I have no regret. I entrust my parents to Your Majesty for their support; by doing so, Your Majesty’s transgressions shall be extinguished and you shall obtain immeasurable merit."
The king said, "Tell me where my parents are; I wish to know this before my son's life is severed.
Śyāma then pointed them out.
"It is not far from this path; you will naturally see a thatched hut where my parents reside.

Your Majesty, proceed slowly so as not to startle or terrify my parents. Using skillful means, explain my intention to them: 'Your Majesty, please inform my parents on my behalf that my time has now come and I am about to depart for the next world.'"

"I do not begrudge my own body or life; rather, I pity my blind parents, who are already advanced in years and have lost their sight. Once I am gone, they will have no one to rely upon, and it is for this reason that I am so distressed and torment myself."

My death is brought about by my own past transgressions; there is no escape from it. Now I repent for all the evils I have committed since having a body throughout incalculable kalpas. May these sins be extinguished here and now. I vow that I and my parents shall meet one another in every lifetime and never be separated. May my parents live out their full natural spans of years without any anxiety or calamity. May devas, nāgas, and spirits constantly follow, protect, and assist them, so that disasters and misfortunes are eliminated, and whatever they desire is fulfilled according to their wishes, spontaneously and without effort.
The King took several attendants and went to his parents' abode; after the King had departed, Śyāma suddenly died.
Hundreds of birds and beasts gathered from all directions like clouds, wailing loudly as they circled above Śyāma’s corpse, licking the blood on his chest.
Hearing this sound, the blind parents became even more terrified and stood there wandering restlessly.
As the King traveled swiftly, he brushed against the grasses and trees, causing them to rustle;
the parents cried out in alarm, "Who is this person?"
"This is not the conduct of my son.
The king said, "I am the King of Kāśī.
Having heard that a blind ascetic was practicing the Way in the mountains, I have come to make offerings to him."
The blind parents said, "We have troubled Your Majesty to come and comfort us, traveling so far to this humble wilderness. We fear you must be utterly exhausted; is your person at ease?"
Are the palace ladies, the crown prince, and the officials all well?
Are the winds and rains harmonious, and are the five grains abundant?
Do the people of neighboring states not inflict harm upon one another?
The king replied to the practitioner,
"I have been graced by your venerable kindness and have always remained in peace.
He then inquired further:
"In this mountain, you have undergone great toil and hardship; amidst these trees, it is very difficult to find rest. Are you at peace?

The blind parents replied, "By the grace of the Great King, we are always at peace. We have a filial son named Śyāma, who constantly gathers fruits, melons, and spring water so that we never lack for anything."
"I have a grass mat; Your Majesty may sit upon it, and there are fruits and melons to eat.
Śyama has gone to fetch water and will return shortly.
When the King heard the words of the blind parents, his heart was once again deeply pained, and he wept as he spoke these words:
"My transgression is indeed grave. Having entered the mountains to hunt, I saw a herd of deer by the water from afar; drawing my bow, I shot at them, but my arrow mistakenly struck Śyama.
Now that the ascetic’s son Śyama has been pierced by the poisoned arrow and his pain is most excruciating, I have come here myself to speak to the ascetic."

Upon hearing this, the parents threw themselves to the ground, their bodies collapsing like the fall of Mount Tai, causing the earth to tremble violently. Wailing and looking up to heaven, they lamented, saying:
"Our son, Śyāma, was the most filial in all the world; none could surpass him. He walked upon the earth always fearing it might suffer pain; for what crime has he been shot and killed?"
Just now, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing down and breaking the trees; the hundred birds cried out in sorrow, their loud wailing shaking the entire mountain.

Having lived in this mountain for over twenty years, I have never before witnessed such a calamitous anomaly. Now that my son Śyāma has gone to fetch water and does not return, I fear there must be some cause for it; all the deities are startled, trembling with solemn awe.
The mother then wept and wailed, refusing to stop; the father said, "Cease for now!
Among those born into this world, who is there that does not die?"
"Impermanence has arrived; it cannot be averted.
He then asked the king, "Where did you shoot Śyāma? Is he dead or alive now?"
The king related Śyāma’s words to his parents; hearing these words from the king, the blind parents were again overcome with profound grief and despair, saying:
"If we suddenly lose our son, we too shall both die."
"Great King!
Now lead us two to our son's corpse.

The king immediately led the blind parents to the corpse; the father embraced his head while the mother took both legs onto her knees. Each used both hands to feel for Śyāma’s arrows, looking up at heaven and crying out:
"The various devas, nāgas, spirits of the mountains, and spirits of the trees all know that my son, Śyāma, was the most filial in the world."
"I am already old and my eyes can no longer see; it would be no regret for me to die in place of my son so that Śyāma may live.
Thereupon, the parents together made this vow:
"If Śyāma’s supreme filial piety is known to Heaven and Earth, then the arrow shall be pulled out, the poisonous pain shall be removed, and Śyāma shall be restored to life."

"Then, the throne of the second Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately shook. Seeing with his own eyes these two blind practitioners of the Way embracing their son and wailing, he heard that from the fourth Tuṣita Heaven, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings came down from the celestial realm. In the time it takes a man to bend and extend his arm, they arrived before Śyāma and poured divine, wondrous medicine into his mouth. As the medicine entered Śyāma’s mouth, the arrow was extracted and the poison expelled; he was restored to life as he had been before."

When the parents heard that Śyāma had died and been restored to life, both their eyes opened; birds and beasts all let out sounds of great joy; the wind ceased and the clouds dispersed so that the sun shone with renewed brilliance; flowing springs gushed forth, pure and cool; lotus flowers of five colors bloomed in the pond with radiant clarity; sandalwood and various incenses mingled, and the trees flourished with a fragrance twice that of usual times.
At that time, the king was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself. He prostrated before Śakra, Lord of Devas, and then returned to bow before his parents and their son, Śyāma, saying:

"I wish to offer all the wealth and treasures of this entire kingdom to these practitioners of the Way, so that we may provide for one another and cause my transgressions to be extinguished forever without remainder."
Śyāma said to the king:
"If you wish to cultivate merit, Your Majesty should simply return to your kingdom and comfort your people, ensuring they uphold the precepts.
Do not engage in hunting or recklessly kill the innocent; otherwise, your person will find no peace, and at the end of your life, you shall enter the hells."

When people dwell in this world, affection and love are but temporary; separation lasts long and they cannot remain forever. Your Majesty, having merit from past lives, has now become king; do not be arrogant in your sovereignty. Because of such sovereignty, you may commit immeasurable evils, which will lead you later into the evil realms—what benefit would there be in regretting it then?
The King replied, "As you have instructed.

The King's hunters, seeing that Śyāma had died, obtained the medicine of the devas so that he died and was reborn; his parents' eyes were opened by such a divine transformation. They all received the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome deeds; upon death, they attained birth in heaven and did not enter the evil realms.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"O you who have gathered here!
He who was Śyāma in his past lives was none other than my own self."
The blind father was King Śuddhodana;
the blind mother was Queen Māyā, the current king’s consort;
and the King of the Kāśī country was Ānanda.
"The Lord of Devas, Śakra, is none other than Maitreya Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In my past lives, as a son I was filial and respectful; as a ruler I was compassionate and nurturing; as a subject I was reverent and devoted. It was through these deeds that I attained the status of the Honored One of the Three Realms."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Son Śyāma.
